\chapter{Two Pointers}
\label{ch:two_pointers}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced, colback=white, colframe=secondaryblue, boxrule=1pt, arc=2mm]
\textbf{\large\textcolor{primaryblue}{Two indices that only move forward turn $\bigO{n^2}$ pair searches into one linear pass --- if you can prove a pointer never needs to come back.}}
\end{tcolorbox}

\chapterfacts{1000}{1700}{6}{12}{30}

\begin{plannedbox}[Planned Contents --- this chapter is not written yet]
\textbf{Part A --- Lessons}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, label=\textbf{A\arabic*.}, itemsep=1pt]
    \item The two-pointer invariant: what the region between, left of and right of the pointers means
    \item Opposite ends on a sorted array: why discarding one end is safe
    \item Fixing one element and running two pointers on the rest: 3-sum, $k$-sum and their complexity
    \item Merging two sorted arrays: from the front, from the back, in place (the gap method); union, intersection and difference of sorted arrays
    \item Same-direction pointers for counting pairs: monotone predicates and the "for each right, how many left" view
    \item Runs: the group pointer that jumps over a block of equal (or consecutive) elements
\end{enumerate}
